prompt: A start-up launches a cheaper, AI-based tax-filing app. Using the competitor analysis and the drivers of competitive behaviour (awareness, motivation, ability), assess how likely the market leader is to respond.
modelAnswer: Market similarity: high if the start-up targets the leader's core customers (individual tax filers), lower if it focuses on young first-time filers the leader does not serve. Resource similarity: moderate – both use software, but the leader has brand, distribution, data and compliance know-how; the start-up has AI capabilities. Awareness: the leader may underestimate the entrant because of routines and past success, or because AI is a sudden technological change. Motivation: low at first (small revenues at stake), rising as the start-up wins its customers or threatens prices (cannibalization). Ability: high – resources to add AI features, cut prices or acquire the start-up. Conclusion: a delayed but strong response is likely once the threat becomes visible; the start-up should avoid head-on overlap (differentiate / noncustomers) for as long as possible.
keyPoints: Conclusion on likelihood and timing of response

prompt: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of being a first mover, and explain how the velocity of the market affects them.
modelAnswer: Advantages: high market shares, secured customer loyalty, authenticity and reputation as the original. Disadvantages: uncertainty about demand, high costs of innovation and learning by trial and error, lower initial quality, risk of path dependency and rigid routines that make the pioneer look traditional later. Velocity: in fast-cycle markets (rapid technological change, short product life cycles) first movers can gain an edge if they keep adapting and moving quickly. In slow-cycle markets, imitation is slow and costly anyway and first movers have no advantage – a fast second can learn from the pioneer's mistakes at lower cost.
keyPoints: Disadvantages (uncertainty, learning costs, quality, path dependency)
